words.definition: the percentage change in population size over a given period
words.example: Population growth rate depends on births, deaths and migration.

words.definition: the annual number of live births per thousand people in a population
words.example: A falling crude birth rate can slow natural population increase.

words.definition: the annual number of deaths per thousand people in a population
words.example: An ageing population may have a relatively high crude death rate.

words.definition: the average number of children a woman would have over her lifetime under current age-specific fertility rates
words.example: Total fertility rate tends to decline with urbanization and female education in many societies.

words.definition: the fertility level at which a population replaces itself from one generation to the next without migration
words.example: Replacement fertility is slightly above two children per woman in many low-mortality populations.

words.definition: the number of deaths of infants under one year of age per thousand live births
words.example: Improved sanitation and healthcare can reduce infant mortality rate.

words.definition: the average number of years a person is expected to live under current mortality conditions
words.example: Life expectancy often increases as healthcare and living conditions improve.

words.definition: a graph showing the age and sex structure of a population
words.example: A broad-based population pyramid indicates a large proportion of young people.

words.definition: the number of people in dependent age groups relative to the working-age population
words.example: Population ageing can increase the old-age dependency ratio.

words.definition: a model describing typical changes in birth and death rates as societies develop
words.example: The demographic transition model links declining mortality and fertility to stages of development.

words.definition: population growth from births minus deaths, excluding migration
words.example: A population can have positive natural increase even while net migration is negative.

words.definition: the period required for a population growing at a constant rate to double in size
words.example: A high growth rate produces a shorter doubling time.

words.definition: continued population growth after fertility falls because a large young generation enters reproductive ages
words.example: Population momentum can keep total population rising after replacement fertility is reached.

words.definition: movement of people from one place of residence to another
words.example: Migration can change both the size and age structure of a population.

words.definition: movement of people into a country or region to live there
words.example: Immigration can offset population decline in an ageing society.

words.definition: movement of people out of a country or region to live elsewhere
words.example: High emigration of young adults can reduce the local workforce.

words.definition: the difference between immigration and emigration relative to population size
words.example: A positive net migration rate increases population independently of births and deaths.

words.definition: a government policy intended to encourage higher birth rates
words.example: Childcare subsidies may form part of a pronatalist policy.

words.definition: a government policy intended to reduce birth rates
words.example: Access to family planning can support an antinatalist policy.

words.definition: potential economic benefit arising when the working-age population is large relative to dependants
words.example: Countries can gain a demographic dividend if education and employment expand as fertility declines.

words.definition: increase in the proportion of a population living in towns and cities
words.example: Industrialization often accelerates urbanization.

words.definition: a city considered as an interacting system of people, infrastructure, energy, materials and environmental processes
words.example: An urban system imports food and energy while exporting wastes.

words.definition: the flows of energy, water, materials and wastes through a city
words.example: Measuring urban metabolism can reveal opportunities to reduce resource use.

words.definition: organized decision-making about land use, transport, housing, infrastructure and public space
words.example: Urban planning can reduce car dependence by placing homes near services.

words.definition: division of urban land into areas designated for particular uses or development rules
words.example: Land-use zoning may separate heavy industry from residential neighbourhoods.

words.definition: low-density outward expansion of a city into surrounding rural or undeveloped land
words.example: Urban sprawl can increase road use and habitat loss.

words.definition: an urban form with relatively high density, mixed uses and efficient public transport
words.example: A compact city can shorten travel distances.

words.definition: an urban area designed to reduce environmental impacts while supporting long-term social and economic well-being
words.example: A sustainable city may combine efficient buildings, green space and public transport.

words.definition: an urban area using digital technologies and data to improve services, efficiency and management
words.example: Smart-city sensors can optimize traffic signals and energy use.

words.definition: a connected network of vegetation, soils and water features that provides ecosystem services in urban areas
words.example: Green roofs and urban wetlands are forms of green infrastructure.

words.definition: previously developed land that is vacant, underused or sometimes contaminated
words.example: Redeveloping a brownfield site can reduce pressure to build on farmland.

words.definition: previously undeveloped land, often outside the existing built-up area
words.example: Housing on a greenfield site can increase habitat loss and commuting.

words.definition: shared passenger transport such as buses, trains and metro systems
words.example: Reliable public transport can reduce private car use.

words.definition: dense mixed-use development designed around high-capacity public transport stations
words.example: Transit-oriented development places housing and services within walking distance of rail stations.

words.definition: urban development combining housing, shops, offices or other functions within the same area
words.example: Mixed-use development can reduce the need for long car journeys.

words.definition: the tendency for built-up areas to be warmer than surrounding rural areas
words.japanese: 都市ヒートアイランド
words.example: Dark surfaces and limited vegetation intensify the urban heat island.

words.definition: the capacity of a city to withstand, adapt to and recover from shocks and stresses
words.example: Floodable parks can improve urban resilience to extreme rainfall.

words.definition: a residential area developed outside formal planning or land-tenure systems, often with limited services
words.japanese: インフォーマル居住地
words.example: Residents of informal settlements may lack secure water and sanitation.

words.definition: neighbourhood change involving rising investment and property values that can displace lower-income residents
words.japanese: ジェントリフィケーション
words.example: New transport links can accelerate gentrification around stations.

words.definition: planned redevelopment or improvement of older urban areas
words.example: Urban renewal can improve infrastructure but may also raise housing costs.

words.definition: presence of substances in the atmosphere at concentrations that harm health, ecosystems or materials
words.example: Traffic and industry are major sources of urban air pollution.

words.definition: a contaminant emitted directly from a source into the atmosphere
words.example: Carbon monoxide from vehicle exhaust is a primary pollutant.

words.definition: a contaminant formed in the atmosphere through chemical reactions involving other substances
words.example: Ground-level ozone is a secondary pollutant.

words.definition: tiny solid particles and liquid droplets suspended in air
words.example: Particulate matter can penetrate the respiratory system.

words.definition: airborne particles with aerodynamic diameters of 2.5 micrometres or less
words.example: Long-term exposure to PM2.5 is associated with cardiovascular and respiratory disease.

words.definition: airborne particles with aerodynamic diameters of 10 micrometres or less
words.example: Road dust contributes to urban PM10 concentrations.

words.definition: a pungent gas produced mainly by burning sulfur-containing fuels and some industrial processes
words.example: Sulfur dioxide can contribute to acid deposition.

words.definition: reactive nitrogen-oxygen gases produced especially by high-temperature combustion
words.example: Vehicle engines are a major urban source of nitrogen oxides.

words.definition: a colourless toxic gas formed by incomplete combustion
words.example: Poorly ventilated combustion can produce dangerous carbon monoxide levels.

words.definition: an organic chemical that readily evaporates and can participate in atmospheric reactions
words.example: Fuel vapours release volatile organic compounds into urban air.

words.definition: polluted air formed when sunlight drives reactions among nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds
words.example: Sunny cities with heavy traffic can experience photochemical smog.

words.definition: transfer of acidic substances from the atmosphere to Earth's surface in wet or dry form
words.example: Sulfur and nitrogen emissions can contribute to acid deposition far from their sources.

words.definition: an atmospheric condition in which warmer air overlies cooler surface air and suppresses vertical mixing
words.example: A temperature inversion can trap pollutants close to the ground.

words.definition: harmful contamination of air inside buildings
words.example: Smoke from solid-fuel cooking can cause severe indoor air pollution.

words.definition: a standardized scale summarizing current air-pollution levels and associated health risk
words.example: Authorities may warn vulnerable people when the air quality index becomes unhealthy.

words.definition: illness affecting the lungs or airways
words.example: Long-term exposure to polluted air can increase respiratory disease.

words.definition: a vehicle exhaust-control device that converts harmful gases into less harmful substances
words.example: Catalytic converters reduce carbon monoxide and nitrogen-oxide emissions from cars.

words.definition: a pollution-control device that removes gases or particles from industrial exhaust
words.example: Power stations can use scrubbers to remove sulfur dioxide.

words.definition: a device that uses electrical charges to remove particles from exhaust gases
words.example: An electrostatic precipitator can capture fine ash before flue gas is released.

words.definition: an urban area where access by high-polluting vehicles is restricted or charged
words.example: A low-emission zone can encourage cleaner vehicles and reduce roadside pollution.
